title: Letters to his Friends
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
source: Translated by Claude from phi0474.phi056.perseus-lat1, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.

passages.original: vehementer etiam res ipsa publica me movit, quae mihi videbatur contentionem, praesertim maximis rebus a Caesare gestis, cum illis viris nolle fieri et, ne fieret, vehementer recusare. gravissime autem me in hac mente impulit et Pompei fides, quam de me Caesari dederat, et fratris mei, quam Pompeio. erant praeterea haec animadvertenda in civitate, quae sunt apud Platonem nostrum scripta divinitus, quales in re publica principes essent, talis reliquos solere esse civis. tenebam memoria nobis consulibus ea fundamenta iacta iam ex K. Ianuariis confirmandi senatus, ut neminem mireari oporteret Nonis Decembri tantum vel animi fuisse in illo ordine vel auctoritatis, idemque memineram nobis privatis usque ad Caesarem et Bibulum consules, cum sententiae nostrae magnum in senatu pondus haberent, unum fere e sensum fuisse bonorum omnium.
passages.english: The state itself also moved me strongly: it seemed to me not to want a contest with those men, especially after Caesar's very great achievements, and to refuse strongly to let one happen. But what pushed me most heavily into this frame of mind was the pledge Pompey had given Caesar concerning me, and the pledge my brother had given Pompey. Besides, there was this to be noticed in the state, which our Plato wrote so divinely: that as the leading men in a commonwealth are, so the rest of the citizens tend to be. I remembered that in my consulship the foundations for strengthening the senate had been laid from the first of January onward, so that no one ought to wonder that on the Nones of December that order showed so much courage or so much authority; and I remembered too that while I was a private citizen, right up to the consulship of Caesar and Bibulus, when my opinions carried great weight in the senate, all good men had been of practically one mind.
passages.notes: 'mireari' read as 'mirari', 'Decembri' as 'Decembribus', 'e sensum' as 'sensum'; scanning errors.

passages.original: Bis ad te scripsi me purgans diligenter, te leviter accusans in eo, quod de me cito credidisses. quod genus querelae mihi quidem videbatur esse amici; sin tibi displicet, non utar eo posthac. sed si, ut scribis, eae litterae non fuerunt 'disertae,' scito meas non fuisse. ut enim Aristarchus Homeri versum negat, quem non probat, sic tu (libet enim mihi iocari), quod disertum non erit, ne putaris meum. vale et in censura, si iam es censor, ut spero, de proavo multum cogitato tuo.
passages.english: Twice I have written to you, carefully clearing myself and lightly accusing you of having been quick to believe [things] about me. That kind of complaint seemed to me, at least, a friend's; but if it displeases you, I will not use it hereafter. But if, as you write, that letter was not 'well-phrased', know that it was not mine. For just as Aristarchus denies that a line of Homer which he does not approve is Homer's, so you (I feel like joking) must not think anything that is not well-phrased to be mine. Farewell, and in your censorship, if you are censor by now, as I hope, think a great deal about your great-grandfather.

passages.original: atque hoc praestantius mihi fuerit et ad laetitiam animi et ad memoriae dignitatem, si in tua scripta pervenero quam si in ceterorum, quod non ingenium mihi solum suppeditatum fuerit tuum, sicut Timoleonti a Timaeo aut ab Herodoto Themistocli, sed etiam auctoritas clarissimi et spectatissimi viri et in rei p. maximis gravissimisque causis cogniti atque in primis probati, ut mihi non solum praeconium, quod, cum in Sigeum venisset, Alexander ab Homero Achilli tributum esse dixit, sed etiam grave testimonium impertitum clari hominis magnique videatur. placet enim Hector ille mihi Naevianus, qui non tantum 'laudari' se laetatur, sed addit etiam 'a laudato viro.'
passages.english: And it will be more distinguished for me, both for my heart's joy and for the dignity of my memory, to have entered your writings than those of others, because I shall have been supplied not only with your talent, as Timoleon was by Timaeus or Themistocles by Herodotus, but also with the authority of a most famous and highly regarded man, known and approved above all in the greatest and weightiest affairs of state; so that I shall seem to have been granted not only the proclamation which Alexander, when he came to Sigeum, said Homer had bestowed on Achilles, but also the weighty testimony of a famous and great man. For I like that Hector of Naevius, who rejoices not merely to be 'praised' but adds 'by a praised man.'

passages.original: Sili causam te docui. is postea fuit apud me. Cum ei dicerem tibi videri sponsionem illam nos sine periculo facere posse, 'SI BONORVM TVRPILIAE POSSESSIONEM Q. CAEPIO PRAETOR EX EDICTO SVO MIHI DEDIT,' negare aiebat Servium tabulas testamenti esse eas, quas instituisset is qui factionem testamenti non habuerit; hoc idem Ofilium dicere; tecum se locutum negabat meque rogavit ut se et causam suam tibi commendarem. nec vir melior, mi Testa, nec mihi amicior P.
passages.english: I have explained Silius' case to you. Afterwards he was at my house. When I told him that you thought we could make that wager without risk, 'IF Q. CAEPIO THE PRAETOR, IN ACCORDANCE WITH HIS EDICT, GAVE ME POSSESSION OF TURPILIA'S GOODS,' he said that Servius denies that a document drawn up by someone who did not have the legal capacity to make a will counts as a will; and that Ofilius says the same. He said he had not spoken with you, and he asked me to commend him and his case to you. There is no better man, my dear Testa, nor anyone more friendly to me, than P.
passages.notes: The sentence continues into the following passage ('Silio', i.e. 'P. Silius').

passages.original: Cum decimum iam diem graviter ex intestinis laborarem neque iis qui mea opera uti volebant me probarem non valere, quia febrim non haberem, fligi in Tusculanum, cum quidem biduum ita ieiunus fuissem ut ne aquam quidem gustarem. itaque confectus languore et fame magis tuum officium desideravi quam a te requiri putavi meum. ego autem quom omnis morbos reformido tum in quo Epicurum tuum Stoici male accipiunt, quia dicat 'straggourika\ kai\ dusenterika\ pa/qh' sibi molesta esse; quorum alterum morbum edacitatis esse putant, alterum etiam turpioris intemperantiae. sanedusenteri/an pertimueram; sed visa est mihi vel loci mutatio vel animi etiam relaxatio vel ipsa
passages.english: When for ten days now I had been suffering badly in my bowels, and could not convince those who wanted my services that I was unwell, because I had no fever, I fled to my Tusculan villa, having been so fasting for two days that I did not even taste water. So, worn out by weakness and hunger, I rather missed your attention than supposed that mine was being asked of you. I dread all diseases, but especially the one for which the Stoics treat your Epicurus badly, because he says 'strangurious and dysenteric afflictions' trouble him; the first of which they think a disease of gluttony, the second of an even more shameful intemperance. I had indeed been very afraid of dysentery; but it seemed to me that either the change of place or the relaxing of my mind, or the very
passages.notes: 'fligi' read as 'fugi'. Greek in Beta Code: strangourika kai dusenterika pathē; dusenterian. Passage breaks off mid-sentence.

passages.original: nos enim plane, mi suavissime Volumni, aut nihil sumus aut nobis quidem ipsis displicemus gregalibus illis, quibus te plaudente vigebamus, ami_is, ut etiam, si quando aliquid dignum nostro nomine emisimus, ingemescamus, quod haec 'pinnigero, non armigero in corpore tela exerceantur,' ut ait Philoctetes apud Accium, 'abiecta gloria.'
passages.english: For I, my most delightful Volumnius, am plainly either nothing, or at any rate I am displeased with myself, now that I have lost those comrades, those friends, through whom I flourished while you applauded, so that even if I ever put out something worthy of my name, I groan that these 'weapons are plied on a winged body, not an armed one,' as Philoctetes says in Accius, 'its glory cast away.'
passages.notes: 'ami_is' read as 'amissis' ('having lost'); the text appears damaged here. The Accius quotation is fragmentary and its precise sense uncertain.

passages.original: sed tamen ipse Caesar habet peracre iudicium, et, ut Servius, frater tuus, quem litteratissimum fuisse iudico, facile diceret: 'hic versus Plauti non est, hic est,' quod tritas auris haberet notandis generibus poetarum et consuetudine legendi, sic audio Caesarem, cum volumina iam confecerit a)pofqegma/twn, si quod adferatur ad eum pro meo quod meum non sit reicere solere ;
passages.english: But all the same Caesar himself has a very keen judgement, and just as your brother Servius, whom I consider to have been a most learned man, could easily say 'This line is not Plautus', 'this one is', because he had ears trained by distinguishing the styles of poets and by the habit of reading, so I hear that Caesar, now that he has completed volumes of *apophthegmata* [witty sayings], is in the habit of rejecting anything brought to him as mine that is not mine;

passages.original: cum homine et edaci tibi res est et qui iam aliquid intellegat (o)yimaqei=s autem homines scis quam insolentes sint) ; dediscendae tibi sunt sportellae et artologam tui. nos iam †ex artis tantum habemus, ut Verrium tuum et Camillum (qua munditia homines, qua elegantia!) vocare saepius audeamus. sed vide audaciam ; etiam Hirtio cenam dedi, sine pavone tamen. in ea cena cocus meus praeter ius fervens nihil non potuit imitari.
passages.english: You are dealing with a man who is both a big eater and one who by now understands something (and you know how insolent late-learners are); you must unlearn your little baskets and your bread-and-meat pies. I have now got so much †from art† that I venture rather often to invite your Verrius and Camillus (what refinement in those men, what elegance!). But look at my daring: I have even given Hirtius a dinner, though without a peacock. At that dinner my cook could imitate everything except the hot sauce.
passages.notes: Greek o)yimaqei=s = opsimatheis, 'late learners'. '†ex artis' is marked corrupt by the edition; sense roughly 'so much skill'. 'artologanum' is a kind of bread cake; reading uncertain.

passages.original: qui nisi fuisset, Antoni reditus a Brundisio pestis patriae fuisset. quae deinceps acta sint scire te arbitror. sed redeamus illuc unde devertimus. accipio excusationem tuam de Sempronio ; neque enim statuti quid in tanta perturbatione habere potuisti. nunc hic dies aliam vitam defert, alios mores postulat, ut ait Terentius. quam ob rem, mi Quinte, conscende nobiscum et quidem ad puppim. una navis est iam bonorum omnium, quam quidem nos damus operam ut rectam teneamus, utinam prospero cursu! sed, quicumque venti erunt, ars nostra certe non aberit.
passages.english: If it had not been for him, Antony's return from Brundisium would have been the ruin of the country. What has been done since, I think you know. But let us return to where we digressed. I accept your excuse about Sempronius; for in such great confusion you could have had nothing fixed. Now 'this day brings another life, demands other ways', as Terence says. So, my Quintus, come aboard with us, and indeed to the stern. There is now one ship of all good men, which we are working to keep on a straight course—may it be a prosperous voyage! But whatever the winds are, our skill at least will not be lacking.

passages.original: sed tamen in omnibus novis coniunctionibus interest qualis primus aditus sit et qua commendatione quasi amicitiae fores aperiantur ; quod ego his litteris efficere volui ; etsi id ipsa per se necessitudo quaesturae effecisse debet ; sed tamen nihilo infirmius illud hoc addito. cura igitur, si me tanti facis quanti et Varro existimat et ipse sentio, ut quam primum intellegam hanc meam commendationem tantum illi utilitatis attulisse quantum et ipse sperarit nec ego dubitarim.
passages.english: But still, in all new connections it matters what the first approach is like and with what recommendation the doors, so to speak, of friendship are opened; this is what I wanted to achieve with this letter, although the bond of the quaestorship should by itself have achieved it; but still, it is none the weaker for this addition. Take care, therefore, if you value me as highly as Varro thinks and as I myself feel, that I learn as soon as possible that this recommendation of mine has brought him as much advantage as he himself hoped and as I did not doubt.

passages.original: T. Manlium, qui negotiatur Thespiis, vehementer diligo ; nam et semper me coluit diligentissimeque observavit et a studiis nostris non abhorret. accedit eo quod Varro Murena magno opere eius causa vult omnia ; qui tamen existimavit, etsi suis litteris, quibus tibi Manlium commendabat, valde confideret, tamen mea commendatione aliquid accessionis fore. me quidem cum Manli familiaritas tum Varronis studium commovit ut ad te quam accuratissime scriberem.
passages.english: I am very fond of T. Manlius, who does business at Thespiae; for he has always paid me attention and shown me the most careful respect, and he is not averse to our studies. Added to this is the fact that Varro Murena is greatly eager for everything on his behalf; yet he thought that, although he had great confidence in his own letter in which he recommended Manlius to you, my recommendation would still add something. For my part, both my friendship with Manlius and Varro's eagerness moved me to write to you as carefully as possible.

passages.original: 'laetus sum laudari me,' inquit Hector, opinor, apud Naevium 'abs te, pater, a laudato viro.' ea est enim profecto iucunda laus, quae ab iis proficiscitur qui ipsi in laude vixerunt. ego vero vel gratulatione litterarum tuarum vel testimoniis sententiae dictae nihil est quod me non adsecutum putem, idque mihi cum amplissimum tum gratissimum est, te libenter amicitiae dedisse quod liquido veritati dares.
passages.english: 'I am glad to be praised,' says Hector, I believe, in Naevius, 'by you, father, a praised man.' For that praise is truly pleasant which comes from those who have themselves lived in praise. For my part, whether through the congratulation of your letter or the testimony of the opinion you delivered [in the senate], there is nothing I do not think I have attained; and this is both most honourable and most gratifying to me, that you gladly granted to friendship what you would plainly grant to truth.

passages.original: vix in ipsis tectis et oppidis frigus infirma valetudine vitatur, nedum in mari et via sit facile abesse ab iniuria temporis. yu=xos de\ leptw=| xrwti\ polemiw/taton, inquit Euripides ; cui tu quantum credas nescio ; ego certe singulos eius versus singula eius testimonia puto. effice, si me diligis, ut valeas et ut ad nos firmus ac valens quam primum venias. ama nos et vale.
passages.english: Even indoors and in towns cold is barely avoided in weak health, much less is it easy at sea and on the road to stay clear of the harm of the season. 'Cold is most hostile to thin skin,' says Euripides; how far you trust him I do not know; I certainly consider his individual lines as individual testimonies. If you love me, make sure you get well and come to us strong and healthy as soon as possible. Love us, and farewell.
passages.notes: Greek in Beta Code: psychos de leptōi chroti polemiōtaton.
